prompt:
Let $G$ be a finite nonabelian group with center $Z$.

(a) If $G/Z$ is a $p$-group, for some prime $p$, show that $G$ has a normal Sylow $p$-subgroup and that $p$ divides $|Z|$.

(b) If $G/Z$ is solvable, show that $G$ has a nonidentity normal $p$-subgroup for some prime dividing $|G : Z|$.
answer: (a) For $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$, $G=PZ$, so $P\trianglelefteq G$; if $p\nmid|Z|$ then $G=P\times Z$ and $Z(G)=Z(P)\times Z>Z$. (b) Take a minimal normal subgroup $N/Z$ of $G/Z$, an elementary abelian $p$-group; by (a)'s argument the Sylow $p$-subgroup of $N=PZ$ is normal in $N$, characteristic, hence normal in $G$, and nontrivial.

prompt:
Let $R\subseteq S$ be commutative rings with the same $1$, and suppose that $S$ is finitely generated as an $R$-module.

(a) If an element $r\in R$ is not invertible in $R$, prove that it is not invertible in $S$. HINT. If $r$ is invertible in $S$, consider a polynomial in $R[X]$ having $1/r$ as a root.

(b) If the ideals of $R$ satisfy the ascending chain condition, show that the ideals of $S$ satisfy the ascending chain condition.
answer: (a) $s=r^{-1}\in S$ is integral over $R$ (determinant trick); multiplying $s^n+a_{n-1}s^{n-1}+\dots+a_0=0$ by $r^{n-1}$ gives $s\in R$. (b) $S$ is a finitely generated module over a Noetherian ring, hence a Noetherian $R$-module, and ideals of $S$ are $R$-submodules.

solutions.title: Integrality from finite generation
solutions.body:
**Integrality.** Let $S=Rs_1+\cdots+Rs_k$ and $s\in S$. Write $ss_i=\sum_ja_{ij}s_j$ with $a_{ij}\in R$, i.e. $(sI-A)\mathbf s=0$ for the column $\mathbf s=(s_1,\dots,s_k)^T$. Multiplying by the adjugate of $sI-A$ gives $\det(sI-A)\,s_j=0$ for all $j$; since $1$ is an $R$-combination of the $s_j$, $\det(sI-A)=0$. Expanding, $s$ is a root of the monic polynomial $\det(XI-A)\in R[X]$.

**(a)** Suppose $rs=1$ with $s\in S$. By integrality, $s^n+a_{n-1}s^{n-1}+\cdots+a_1s+a_0=0$ with $a_i\in R$, $n\ge1$. Multiply by $r^{n-1}$ and use $rs=1$:
$$s+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}r+\cdots+a_0r^{n-1}=0,$$
so $s=-(a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}r+\cdots+a_0r^{n-1})\in R$, and $r$ is invertible in $R$ — contradiction.

**(b)** $R$ is Noetherian, so the free module $R^k$ is a Noetherian $R$-module (induction on $k$ using $0\to R^{k-1}\to R^k\to R\to0$), and so is its quotient $S$ (via the surjection $R^k\to S$, $e_i\mapsto s_i$). Every ideal of $S$ is an $R$-submodule of $S$, so an ascending chain of ideals of $S$ is an ascending chain of $R$-submodules and therefore stabilizes. ∎

prompt:
Working in the field of complex numbers, let $\varepsilon$ be a primitive $16^{\text{th}}$ root of unity, and let $\alpha = \varepsilon\sqrt 2$. Set $E = \mathbb Q[\varepsilon]$, where $\mathbb Q$ is the field of rational numbers, let $f(X) = X^8 + 16 \in\mathbb Q[X]$, and note that $\alpha$ is a root of $f(X)$.

(a) Show that $\sqrt 2\in\mathbb Q[\varepsilon^2]$.

(b) Conclude that $f(X)$ splits in $E[X]$.

(c) If $G = \mathrm{Gal}(E/\mathbb Q)$, prove that no nonidentity element of $G$ fixes $\alpha$. Conclude that $f(X)$ is irreducible in $\mathbb Q[X]$.
answer: (a) $\zeta=\varepsilon^2$ is a primitive $8$th root of unity and $(\zeta+\zeta^{-1})^2=2$. (b) The roots of $f$ are $\alpha\varepsilon^{2j}\in E$. (c) $\sigma_k(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^k$ ($k$ odd) fixes $\alpha$ only if $\varepsilon^{k-1}=\pm1$, i.e. $k\in\{1,9\}$, and $\sigma_9$ fixes $\sqrt2\in\mathbb Q[\varepsilon^2]$ so sends $\alpha\mapsto-\alpha$; hence $\mathbb Q(\alpha)=E$ has degree $8=\deg f$.

solutions.title: Galois group of the 16th cyclotomic field
solutions.body:
**(a)** $\zeta=\varepsilon^2$ is a primitive $8$th root of unity, so $\zeta^4=-1$ and $\zeta^{-2}=\zeta^{6}=\zeta^4\zeta^2=-\zeta^{2}$. Hence
$$(\zeta+\zeta^{-1})^2=\zeta^2+2+\zeta^{-2}=2,$$
so $\pm\sqrt2=\zeta+\zeta^{-1}\in\mathbb Q[\varepsilon^2]$, and therefore $\sqrt2\in\mathbb Q[\varepsilon^2]$.

**(b)** By (a), $\alpha=\varepsilon\sqrt2\in E$. Since $\varepsilon^8=-1$, $\alpha^8=\varepsilon^8\cdot16=-16$. For $j=0,\dots,7$, $(\alpha\varepsilon^{2j})^8=\alpha^8\varepsilon^{16j}=-16$, and these $8$ elements are distinct because $\varepsilon^2$ has order $8$. So they are the $8$ roots of $f$, all in $E$, and $f=\prod_{j=0}^7(X-\alpha\varepsilon^{2j})$ splits in $E[X]$.

**(c)** The $16$th cyclotomic polynomial $X^8+1$ is irreducible, so $[E:\mathbb Q]=8$ and $G=\{\sigma_k\mid k\in(\mathbb Z/16)^\times\}$ with $\sigma_k(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^k$. Since $\sqrt2\in E$ and $\sigma_k(\sqrt2)^2=2$, $\sigma_k(\sqrt2)=\pm\sqrt2$.

Suppose $\sigma_k(\alpha)=\alpha$, i.e. $\varepsilon^k\sigma_k(\sqrt2)=\varepsilon\sqrt2$. Then $\varepsilon^{k-1}=\sqrt2/\sigma_k(\sqrt2)=\pm1$, so $\varepsilon^{2(k-1)}=1$ and $8\mid k-1$: $k\in\{1,9\}$. For $k=9$: $\sigma_9(\varepsilon^2)=\varepsilon^{18}=\varepsilon^2$, so $\sigma_9$ fixes $\mathbb Q[\varepsilon^2]\ni\sqrt2$, and $\sigma_9(\alpha)=\varepsilon^9\sqrt2=\varepsilon^8\alpha=-\alpha\ne\alpha$. Hence only $\sigma_1=1$ fixes $\alpha$.

By the Galois correspondence $\mathrm{Gal}(E/\mathbb Q(\alpha))=1$, so $\mathbb Q(\alpha)=E$ and $[\mathbb Q(\alpha):\mathbb Q]=8$. The minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ has degree $8$ and divides the monic degree-$8$ polynomial $f$, so it equals $f$; thus $f$ is irreducible in $\mathbb Q[X]$. ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over the field $F$ of characteristic $p > 0$, let $T\colon V\to V$ be a linear operator on $V$, and set $W = \{v\in V \mid vT = v\}$. Suppose that $T^p = I$, the identity, and that $\dim_F W = 1$.

(a) Show that $(T - I)^p = 0$ and conclude that $\dim_F V \le p$.

(b) If $\dim_F V < p$, prove that $(T - I)^{p-1} = 0$.

(c) If, for some vector $v\in V$, we have $v + vT + vT^2 + \cdots + vT^{p-1} \ne 0$, prove that $\dim_F V = p$.
answer: (a) $(T-I)^p=T^p-I=0$ in characteristic $p$; $N=T-I$ is nilpotent with $\dim\ker N=1$, and $\dim\ker N^k\le k$, so $\dim V\le p$. (b) $N^{\dim V}=0$ and $p-1\ge\dim V$. (c) $1+x+\dots+x^{p-1}=(x-1)^{p-1}$ in $\mathbb F_p[x]$, so $N^{p-1}\ne0$; by (b) $\dim V\ge p$.

solutions.title: The nilpotent operator $T-I$
solutions.body:
Operators act on the right; put $N=T-I$, so $W=\ker N$ and $\dim\ker N=1$.

**(a)** $T$ and $I$ commute, so by the binomial theorem $(T-I)^p=\sum_k\binom pk T^k(-I)^{p-k}=T^p+(-1)^pI$, since $p\mid\binom pk$ for $0<k<p$. If $p$ is odd this is $T^p-I=0$; if $p=2$, $-I=I$ and it is $T^2+I=T^2-I=0$. So $N^p=0$.

For each $k\ge1$, $N$ maps $\ker N^k$ into $\ker N^{k-1}$ with kernel $\ker N$, so $\dim\ker N^k\le\dim\ker N^{k-1}+\dim\ker N=\dim\ker N^{k-1}+1$. By induction $\dim\ker N^k\le k$. Hence $\dim V=\dim\ker N^p\le p$.

**(b)** Let $d=\dim V<p$. The kernels $\ker N^0\subseteq\ker N\subseteq\cdots$ grow strictly until they stabilize, and they reach $V$ (as $N^p=0$); since each strict step increases the dimension, $\ker N^d=V$, i.e. $N^d=0$. As $p-1\ge d$, $N^{p-1}=0$.

**(c)** In $\mathbb F_p[x]$, $(x-1)^p=x^p-1$ (as in (a)), so $(x-1)^{p-1}=\dfrac{x^p-1}{x-1}=1+x+\cdots+x^{p-1}$. Substituting $T$:
$$v+vT+\cdots+vT^{p-1}=v(T-I)^{p-1}=vN^{p-1}.$$
If this is nonzero then $N^{p-1}\ne0$, so by (b) $\dim V\not<p$; with (a), $\dim V=p$. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring with $1$. A (right) $R$-module $V$ is said to be strongly $n$-generated, for some integer $n$, if every submodule of $V$ is generated as an $R$-module by some set of $\le n$ elements.

(a) If $V$ is strongly $n$-generated and if $W$ is a submodule of $V$, prove that both $W$ and $V/W$ are strongly $n$-generated.

(b) Let $W$ be a submodule of $V$. If $W$ is strongly $n$-generated and if $V/W$ is strongly $m$-generated, prove that $V$ is strongly $(n + m)$-generated.

(c) If $V$ has composition length $n$, prove that $V$ is strongly $n$-generated.
answer: (a) Submodules of $W$ are submodules of $V$; submodules of $V/W$ are $U/W$, generated by the images of generators of $U$. (b) For $U\le V$, combine $\le n$ generators of $U\cap W$ with $\le m$ elements of $U$ whose images generate $(U+W)/W$. (c) Induction on the length using (b), simple modules being strongly $1$-generated.

solutions.title: Generators of extensions
solutions.body:
**(a)** Every submodule of $W$ is a submodule of $V$, hence generated by $\le n$ elements; so $W$ is strongly $n$-generated. A submodule of $V/W$ has the form $U/W$ with $W\subseteq U\subseteq V$; if $u_1,\dots,u_k$ ($k\le n$) generate $U$, then $u_1+W,\dots,u_k+W$ generate $U/W$.

**(b)** Let $U\le V$. The submodule $U\cap W$ of $W$ is generated by some $x_1,\dots,x_k$, $k\le n$. The submodule $(U+W)/W$ of $V/W$ is generated by $\le m$ elements, which we may take of the form $u_1+W,\dots,u_l+W$ with $u_j\in U$ (every element of $(U+W)/W$ is $u+W$ with $u\in U$). We claim $U$ is generated by the $x_i$ and $u_j$. Given $u\in U$, write $u+W=\sum_ju_jr_j+W$ with $r_j\in R$. Then $u-\sum_ju_jr_j\in U\cap W$, so it equals $\sum_ix_is_i$, and $u=\sum_ju_jr_j+\sum_ix_is_i$. Hence $U$ is generated by $\le n+m$ elements.

**(c)** Induction on $n$. If $n=0$, $V=0$ and its only submodule is generated by the empty set. If $V$ is simple ($n=1$), its submodules are $0$ and $V=vR$ for any $v\ne0$, so $V$ is strongly $1$-generated. For $n\ge2$ take a composition series $0=V_0\subset\cdots\subset V_n=V$. Then $V_{n-1}$ has length $n-1$, so it is strongly $(n-1)$-generated by induction, and $V/V_{n-1}$ is simple, hence strongly $1$-generated. By (b), $V$ is strongly $n$-generated. ∎
